source.title: Fisher Rank Inflation: A Spectral Signature of Memorization under Label Noise

page_placements.theme: Memorization changes representation, activation and spectral diagnostics

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests memorization dynamics under label corruption, but measures centered last-layer gradient-spectrum rank and leave-one-out attribution rather than whether training images with random labels reach zero training error. It reports eventual near-perfect accuracy on noisy training labels in an appendix, yet does not test the claim's original random-label, chance-test-error, or unchanged-hyperparameter conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports noisy-label training accuracy and test-accuracy findings that bear on the claim, plus gradient-spectrum measurements related to memorization. The Fisher-rank and attribution results do not themselves measure fitting random labels or training error. No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, Gaussian-input, regularization-ablation, or real-label-versus-random-label learning-order experiment is reported. The cited original studies' results are not this study's own results.
record.test_reason: The corruption sweep directly measures training accuracy and clean test accuracy under SGD, bearing on V4 using the original intervention and outcome measures. Appendix A.7.2 also explicitly reports early optimization slowing with greater corruption, bearing on part of V2. The spectral diagnostics alone do not test these versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors conclude that Fisher Rank Inflation accompanies memorization, increases with corruption severity, and is disproportionately supported by corrupted examples across synthetic and human annotation noise. They present it as a spectral signature, with architecture-dependent attribution strength and timing, rather than a universal predictor of overfitting. Their appendix additionally reports near-perfect noisy-label training accuracy, worsening clean test accuracy with corruption, and slower early optimization at higher corruption.
record.recipe_differences: Uses symmetric label corruption on CIFAR image datasets and measures centered last-layer gradient-spectrum effective rank and leave-one-out rank attribution. It does not reproduce the original random-label intervention or its training/test error measures.
record.method_sensitivity: The onset-versus-test-degradation lead-time result depends on architecture and threshold choice: for ViT some threshold pairs produce non-positive lead time, while the tested convolutional settings remain positive across the grid.

fits_no_version.finding: Peak Fisher effective rank increases from 28.88 ± 1.95 without corruption to 97.09 ± 1.78 at 60% corruption.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing symmetric label corruption increases peak effective rank of centered last-layer gradient scatter in this setting.

fits_no_version.finding: At a representative peak-rank checkpoint, corrupted examples have mean rank contribution 0.0125 versus −0.0056 for clean examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Corrupted examples contribute disproportionately to gradient-spectrum rank inflation at peak-rank checkpoints.

record.problems: The paper evaluates a fixed training subset of 20,000 examples and computes Fisher trajectories on deterministic subsets of 4,096 or 2,048 examples; leave-one-out analyses use 2,048 examples. The corruption-severity sweep has three seeds. The main evidence for training accuracy and clean test-accuracy trends is in figures with qualitative prose and no exact values in the text. The paper explicitly says broader validation across larger models, alternative modalities, and structured or instance-dependent corruption remains necessary.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for the six claim versions: the study's other reported results concern Fisher-rank trajectories, attribution diagnostics, corruption detection, and lead times rather than those versions' named behaviors. Numerical results in Tables 1–12 are mostly attribution or spectral metrics and do not measure the claim versions' outcomes.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error under that intervention, chance test performance, and preservation of architecture and hyperparameters in that comparison.
The small constant-factor training-time claim and convergence-time ratios against clean-label training; the reported slowdown concerns early optimization only.
All unstructured-input interventions and their training-error outcomes.
Corruption beyond 60%, the completely random-label endpoint, chance-level test performance, and exact zero training error at every corruption rate.
Regularization ablations establishing necessity or sufficiency for fitting and generalization.
Direct measurement of clean-versus-corrupted example learning order or real-versus-random label learning trajectories. Spectral transitions and their interpretation do not establish this ordering.

missing.what: Add the explicit qualitative result that greater corruption slows optimization during early training. No convergence-time ratio or numerical slowdown is supplied.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. No result warrants limits_scope or challenges: missing endpoints and unmeasured components remain untested. The main spectral contribution does not negate the appendix's direct behavioral tests. Appendix A.2 specifies a fixed-size corruption subset sampled without replacement, whereas Section 4.1 describes independent replacement; neither protocol produces completely random labels at the tested rates.

versions.untested_parts: The appendix says all noisy settings eventually approach near-perfect training accuracy on provided labels, but gives no exact accuracy values in the supplied text. It does not state that labels are completely random, that test error is at chance, or that the comparison preserves the original architecture and training hyperparameters.
No comparison of training time or convergence slowdown against true-label training is reported.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment is reported.

The paper sweeps symmetric corruption rates and reports increasing peak Fisher effective rank, eventual near-perfect accuracy on noisy labels, and declining clean test accuracy at higher corruption. It does not report a result for every rate establishing perfect training fit while test error rises steadily toward chance, nor does it directly establish that remaining signal is captured while noise is memorized.
Although training details include augmentation and weight decay, no ablation tests whether these are necessary or sufficient for random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
The paper describes structure learning followed by memorization under label noise, but does not compare learning dynamics for real labels against completely random labels as this version specifies.
